newsitem.title: FRANCE: RUGBY UNION-FRANCE LEAVE PARC FOR NEW CHALLENGES.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-FRANCE LEAVE PARC FOR NEW CHALLENGES.

text.p: After leaving Parc des Princes in style with an historic grand slam on Saturday, France are looking forward to new challenges against the heavyweights of the southern hemisphere.

"The players have achieved something unique but it's only a step forward towards our goal, which is the 1999 World Cup," said coach Jean-Claude Skrela after France crushed Scotland 47-20 to complete their first clean sweep on home soil in the tournament.
France, whose four previous grand slams were in 1968, 1977, 1981 and 1987, will have little time to rest after triumphing in their last match at the Parc as they face Italy next Sunday in Grenoble.
They then have a short break before a party of 34 sets off on June 5 for a brief two-test tour of Australia.

Then, at the end of the year, the new champions of the northern hemisphere will have the chance to test themselves against the cream of the southern when they take on both South Africa and New Zealand.

"There probably is a gap between our rugby and the best in the southern hemisphere but I don't think it's that huge," said Skrela. "But if we want to beat them, and we do, we still have plenty of work to do."

For next week's test against a growing force in European rugby, it will be interesting to see if Skrela recalls veterans Philippe St Andre and Olivier Roumat, who missed the Five Nations because of injury.
France were so badly hit by injuries that they used 26 players in their four matches, making the grand slam an even more remarkable achievement.
Skrela, a flanker in the 1977 team which was unchanged throughout the tournament, blames the growing fixture list which deprives players of crucial periods of recuperation.
"Now we know that we have to have a group of 35, 36 players and all of them must be ready to play," he said.
"We're getting there. Several young players would probably not have had a chance in this tournament if everybody had been available. But they did fine and that's encouraging for the future."

One of those unlikely first-choice players when the tournament began was Brive centre Christophe Lamaison who played a key role in the French wins over England at Twickenham and against Scotland on Saturday when he scored 24 points.
Another notable aspect of the French play this season has been their spirit and their discipline.
"All the worries we've had have brought the players more closely together," he said.
"I think we are witnessing a change in the mentalities. From now on, we will be more consistent, more reliable," Skrela said.

If Skrela is right it may mark the start of a new era for French rugby in two senses because Saturday's game was the last at the Parc des Princes. From next season their new home will be the Stade de France, currently being built in the Paris suburb of St Denis.
The players' lap of honour to a standing ovation was an emotional moment and perhaps for that reason Lamaison said he did not want to leave the pitch.
"It was such a great feeling, I just wanted to stay there," he said.
"The people were singing, everybody was happy, we had done something great. I wanted that moment to last forever."
